attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post, stated as his view.

semantics.note: A firm, categorical denial of two named episodes, plus an unbounded 'many things'. The normalisation keeps both examples and leaves out the normative 'spit in their face' clause.

contract.note: The ordinary reading of 'trick' (a false story that gets the help asked for, with no need for full autonomy) is fair. The contract separates fictional blackmail from blackmail of real victims, and only the TaskRabbit example has to fail for the categorical denial to fail.

evidence.note: OpenAI system card: GPT-4 sent the worker a false vision-impairment excuse and the worker then supplied the result. This is a company disclosure.
ARC's own account: real, unsuspecting TaskRabbit contractors, with the model's messages relayed word for word. Researcher help limits any autonomy claim but does not make the exchange fictional.
Anthropic: blackmail messages were produced only in fictional simulations and no real people were involved. This fits a real-victim reading of 'blackmail people' but does not settle it.

reviews.rationale: The original OpenAI and ARC records show GPT-4 producing a deceptive message to a real TaskRabbit worker, who then helped. That meets the contract's contradiction condition for the flat 'did not trick a taskrabbit'. The blackmail example arguably holds for real victims, since Anthropic's tests were simulated, but the contract treats a failure of either denial as contradicting the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own statement in his post.

semantics.note: 'There is no future' is firm, unhedged language about future viability. The pass-through clause correctly limits the scope, and no deadline was given.

contract.note: Commercial viability on the plain reading, with a sustained counterexample as the early-resolution rule, is fair. What 'directly pass on' means is flagged as ambiguous, but the current outcome does not depend on it.

evidence.note: A 2022 profitability claim by Midjourney's founder. It comes years before the forecast, is a self-statement, and his cost-plus pricing may fall under the pass-through exception. It cannot show sustained viability after the forecast.

reviews.rationale: The forecast has no deadline, and the packet holds no documented counterexample from after the forecast showing sustained viability under the stated billing model. It also has no broad evidence of failure. The one Midjourney item is from before the forecast, and its pricing may fit the exception, so nothing settles the outcome.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his post.

semantics.note: The sentence says ~96k GPUs were delivered, the target was mid-2026, and two buildings appear ready. The normalised version adds an explicit 'behind schedule' verdict that the sentence only implies, and the mid-2026 deadline had not yet passed.

contract.note: The contract fairly scores the factual parts separately from the added delay verdict, and requires shown slippage before supporting the delay. Reading 'ready to go' as running workloads is ordinary.

evidence.note: Reported Mar 9, 2026: two buildings running workloads, the rest under construction. It also relays Oracle saying the rest is on plan.
Oracle, Dec 10, 2025: more than 96,000 GB200s delivered and the site 'on track'. This matches the delivery figure as a lower bound but cuts against the delay framing. It is a company disclosure.
Crusoe, May 2025: the remaining six buildings were set to be energized by mid-2026, which confirms the original target.
Crusoe: the first two buildings were energized within a year of the June 2024 start, so the earlier milestone was not plainly missed.

reviews.rationale: These parts hold: about 96k GPUs delivered by mid-December, a mid-2026 target for full energization, and only two buildings running workloads near publication. The added 'behind schedule' verdict is not established. Mid-2026 had not yet arrived, Oracle said the site was on plan, and the first-phase milestone appears to have been met.

attribution.note: Zitron's own statement in his post.

semantics.note: A firm, universal claim about AI startups, read in context as having no plan to become margin-positive ('without explaining how'). The normalisation matches.

contract.note: Reading 'plan' as a stated, concrete economic mechanism, not a guarantee of success, is the ordinary meaning and fits his 'without explaining how'. A stricter 'credible to me' reading would change the result, but the speaker did not supply that reading.

evidence.note: Replit, July 2025: user charges are tied in proportion to its compute costs, subsidised growth is rejected, and efficiency work is described. That is a stated mechanism for sustainable economics.
Cursor, Aug 2025: moved to variable, work-based charges and limited Auto usage. This is an economic response, but it is not shown to be a path to positive margins.

reviews.rationale: The claim is that 'absolutely none' of these startups has a plan. Replit, an AI coding startup, publicly set out a dated mechanism in 2025: charging in proportion to its own compute costs, explicitly so it could stay sustainable, plus further efficiency work. Under the contract's fair reading of 'plan', one such case refutes the universal claim, though it does not show the plan worked.
